1:
The flight is dated by what Saul was doing at the time. Gill places it while Saul lay bound in a trance at Naioth, prophesying; Clarke gives the simpler motive, that on hearing Saul had come to that place David knew he was no longer safe and fled for his life. Ellicott draws a harder lesson from the episode, that the strange course of events in the prophetic schools by Ramah warned David the home of his old master, the great seer, was no permanent sanctuary where he could safely rest — while still giving him time to get away and take counsel with his friend. Ellicott supposes it was by Samuel's advice that he betook himself once more to the city of Saul, and that the return was evidently secret.

Henry reads the meeting as a providential arrangement. While Saul lay bound by his trance David escaped to the court and got speech with Jonathan, and it was happy for him that he had such a friend at court when he had such an enemy on the throne. From this Henry draws a general consolation: if there are those who hate and despise us, we need not be disturbed, for there are also those who love and respect us, God having set the one over against the other. He characterises Jonathan by two proverbs — a friend that loved at all times, who loved David as well in his distress and made him as welcome in his arms as he had done in the days of triumph, and a brother born for adversity (Proverbs 17:17).

What David actually asks for is narrower than a complaint. Henry notes that he appeals to Jonathan himself concerning his innocence, and needed add scarcely anything by way of proof; what he wanted was that if Jonathan knew of any just offence given to his father he would say so, that David might humble himself and beg pardon. Ellicott describes the same speech as a passionate assertion of entire innocence of the crimes laid to his charge by the unhappy, jealous king, and observes that David's words here are found in substance in not a few of his Psalms, where he maintains in touching language how bitterly the world had wronged and persecuted a righteous man.

Henry also accounts for Jonathan's reluctance before the argument begins. From a principle of filial respect he was very loath to believe his father designed or would ever do so wicked a thing, and the rather because he knew nothing of any such design, having usually been made privy to all Saul's counsels. Henry treats the reluctance as creditable rather than obtuse: as became a dutiful son, Jonathan endeavoured to cover his father's shame so far as was consistent with justice and fidelity to David, and charity is not forward to think evil of any, least of all of a parent (1 Corinthians 13:5). Clarke, for his part, uses the opening verse to lay out the whole shape of the chapter, from the complaint and the renewed covenant to the arrow signal and the affectionate parting.
2:
Jonathan's denial is read as sincere rather than evasive, and each witness supplies a different ground for it. Gill has him unable to believe his father held any such intention, allowing only that if anything of the kind had shown itself it was when Saul was in a frenzy, a melancholy disorder having seized him — the thing being too gross and detestable to be credited. Ellicott puts the same distinction more sharply: Jonathan even now refuses to believe that his father, when he was himself, really wished David ill, and puts all that has happened down to the unhappy malady.

The argument he actually makes rests on his own standing with the king. Keil and Delitzsch render it as a claim about access — his father does not the smallest thing without revealing it to him, so why should he hide this? Ellicott presses the inference: if the king in good earnest had designs on David's life, he would in his calm, lucid days have consulted Jonathan, to whom he ever confided all his State secrets. Clarke adds a second ground, that Jonathan thought his father could have no evil design because of the oath he had sworn on the matter earlier; Wesley makes that the whole of it, saying simply that Jonathan gave credit to his father's oath.

A textual point lies under the English. Ellicott reports that the commentators and the versions — the Septuagint, the Vulgate and the Chaldee — all agree in reading a negative in the Hebrew where the received text has a pronoun, one letter being substituted for another. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same result, taking the particle after the demonstrative to stand for the negative, and preferring the written form to the marginal reading.

Gill and Keil and Delitzsch both read the preceding complaint as a question about charges rather than a plea for mercy. Keil and Delitzsch set out David's position before this exchange: though delivered for the moment from the death that threatened him, through the marvellous influence of the divine inspiration of the prophets upon Saul and his messengers, he could find in that no lasting protection from the plots of a mortal enemy — and so sought his friend and asked what he had done, what his crime and his sin before Jonathan's father were, that Saul should seek his life.
3:
David answers the denial with an oath, and the commentators explain why an oath was needed. Gill has him swearing to remove from Jonathan a doubt he did not feel himself, Jonathan being unwilling to believe his father could be guilty of so foul a crime; Wesley says the same more briefly, that the matter being of great moment and Jonathan doubting its truth, David confirmed his word with an oath. Keil and Delitzsch note it was a second swearing, and that the particle introducing it carries the substance of what was sworn.

The content of the oath is an argument about Saul's silence. Keil and Delitzsch render it that Saul knows David has found favour in Jonathan's eyes and therefore thinks Jonathan shall not know of the plan, lest he be grieved. Ellicott expands the reasoning: David urges that his fall and even his death had been decided upon by a king who, knowing how Jonathan loved him, would shrink from confiding such plans to his son. Wesley reads the clause as an interposed explanation of exactly that — a reason why Saul concealed it from Jonathan. On this account the very absence of warning that Jonathan treats as evidence of innocence becomes, in David's hands, evidence of design.

Ellicott draws the contrast between the two men out of the exchange. David, with his clear, bright intellect, had looked deeper into Saul's heart than the heroic, guileless son, and recognised only too vividly the intensity of the king's hatred; Keil and Delitzsch make the same judgment in a phrase, that David had looked deeper into Saul's heart. Ellicott adds the outcome, that the mournful earnestness of the son of Jesse had its effect upon the prince, who consented to make the public trial of his father's real mind that his friend asked for.

The closing image attracts a classical parallel. Keil and Delitzsch render it literally as about a step between David and death; Clarke paraphrases it as a life in the most imminent danger and finds the same figure in Juvenal, who, satirising those who risk their lives for gain on perilous voyages, bids a man go and commit his life to the winds, trusting to a hewn plank four or seven fingers thick — if the beam it was cut from was large enough. Keil and Delitzsch then record Jonathan's reply, that whatever David's soul says he will do for him, and note that it is this undertaking which the next request takes up.
4:
Jonathan's undertaking is read as a change of position. Gill has him now giving credit to what David had said, and speaking in order to comfort and support him under his apprehensions of danger; Keil and Delitzsch render the promise as a blank cheque — what David's soul says, Jonathan will do, that is, fulfil every wish. Gill describes the plan David then proposes as a method for making trial of the disposition of Saul's mind towards him, which is what turns a private reassurance into a test.

The feast David must absent himself from is explained from the calendar. Clarke sets out the framework: the months of the Hebrews were lunar and reckoned from new moon to new moon, and because their other feasts, the passover in particular, were counted from these, they were very scrupulous in observing each new moon's first appearance. On these days sacrifices were offered and a feast held (Numbers 10:10; Numbers 28:11), and Clarke supposes families feasted together on such occasions, while the gathering of all the families of a whole tribe seems to have happened only once a year.

Keil and Delitzsch draw a further inference from the arithmetic of David's proposal. Because he reckons to the third evening and means to hide on the new moon's day and the day after it, the festival cannot have been merely the religious observance the law prescribes but must have been kept as a civil festival too, and in that character for two days — a conclusion they say is confirmed still more clearly by the later verses in which Saul expects David at table. Wesley reads the same phrase narrowly, taking the third day as the next day but one after the new moon, and is careful about what David did not say: his meaning was not that he would hide in one certain place for all three days, but that he would secure himself, whether at Bethlehem among his friends or elsewhere, until then.

Ellicott fills in what the occasion would have looked like at court, and uses it to explain a later detail. The feast seems to have been carefully observed, doubtless with the blast of trumpets and with solemn burnt offerings and sin offerings — which is why, when the moment comes, the plea of possible ceremonial uncleanness is accepted at once as an excuse for absence. The rites were accompanied by a banquet both of state and of family, at which David was expected as the king's son-in-law and as the holder of a high post in the royal army. Ellicott closes on the gap between the two friends: Jonathan persisted in treating his father's designs as frenzied acts incident upon his malady, and evidently believed that after the seizure at Ramah Saul would return and meet David with the confidence of old days, whereas David believed otherwise.
6:
The excuse David supplies is a real custom, and the commentators explain both the custom and its irregularity. Keil and Delitzsch take the ground of excuse to show that families and households were accustomed to keep united sacrificial feasts once a year, and note that by the law these ought to have been kept at the tabernacle; but at this time, the central sanctuary having fallen into disuse, they were held wherever there were altars of Jehovah — Bethlehem among them. Ellicott gives the same account and dates the lapse precisely, to the destruction of the Tabernacle of Shiloh, after which such feasts were most probably held in tribal centres. He quotes von Gerlach to the effect that in the then disorganised condition of public worship, which David was the first to give regular form, family usages of this sort had established themselves after the manner of other nations, contrary to the prescriptions concerning the unity of Divine worship.

Whether David's excuse was a lie, and whether that matters, divides them openly. Keil and Delitzsch state it flatly: we see from these words that David did not look upon prevarication as a sin. Ellicott concedes the fact and withholds the approval — it is highly probable the festival was indeed being held at Bethlehem at this time, but clear that David did not purpose being present at it, so the excuse was a feigned one; and he adds that the morality of the request is by no means sanctioned by the compiler of the history, who simply relates the story. Gill's note stays on the surface of the wording, glossing the condition as Saul diligently inquiring after him, and Wesley explains why the excuse was plausible in Jonathan's mouth: as the king's son and deputy he was accustomed to give military men leave to depart for a season upon just occasions.

The test is then stated as a pair of outcomes. Keil and Delitzsch render the first as peace — if Saul says it is well, he cherishes no murderous thoughts — and the second as a settled purpose, the verb meaning to be completed and so to be firmly and unalterably determined. Gill reads the first branch as a judgment on Saul rather than on David's safety, that it would be very good and right in him to answer so.

How much David already knew is argued over in the commentary itself. Keil and Delitzsch report that Seb. Schmidt inferred from the closing words that the fact was certain enough to David though not to Jonathan, and that Thenius observed, in their view much more correctly, that it is perfectly obvious David was not quite clear as to Saul's intentions. They add that Thenius thereby upsets his own earlier assertion that after what David had gone through he could never have thought of sitting at the king's table as before — so the same clause is used to settle the question and to expose an inconsistency in settling it.
8:
The request rests on an existing bond, and the force of the appeal lies in how that bond is described. Keil and Delitzsch note that David made sure Jonathan would grant it on account of their friendship, since Jonathan had brought him into a covenant of Jehovah with himself; and they explain the title, that David calls their covenant of friendship a covenant of Jehovah because it had been made with a solemn invocation of the divine name. Wesley expands the same point into a definition: a solemn covenant, not lightly undertaken but seriously entered into in the name and fear of God and in his presence, calling him to be witness of their sincerity and the avenger of perfidiousness in whichever of them should break it. What David asks under it is practical — Gill has him seeking only to be told how his father's mind stood affected, so that he might conduct himself accordingly, either appearing at court or providing for his safety by flight; Wesley puts it as timely notice and a true account of Saul's disposition.

The clause David adds is an offer of his own life, and the witnesses take it as a way of forcing the issue. Keil and Delitzsch read it as a device to make the fulfilment of the request quite certain, the pronoun being used to strengthen the appeal: if there is a fault in David, let Jonathan kill him himself. Clarke states the condition in terms of the charges, that if Jonathan sees him plotting against the state or against his father's life he should strike the blow. Wesley renders the consent plainly and then turns the second half into a question of loyalty — why should Jonathan betray him to his father by concealing Saul's evil intentions from him? Keil and Delitzsch supply the unspoken end of that question, that the bringing to Saul would be for the purpose of death.

Ellicott uses the mention of the covenant to raise a question about the narrative itself. It may seem strange, he says, that these last meetings of David and Jonathan are told in such detail, with the speakers' very words quoted and so many apparently trivial circumstances related; and one might ask how the compiler came by so intimate an acquaintance with what passed when David was alone with Jonathan. His answer to the first difficulty is the interest of the readers — never forgetting how intensely interesting to the chosen people were all the circumstances of their loved king's life, nor the deathless interest with which they would hear of David's rise through great suffering and long trial to the throne.

He then explains why this particular stretch is given at length, and offers a conjecture about its source. This period was the turning-point of a grand career: from this moment David's way diverged from the every-day life of ordinary duty and prosperity and became, for a long and weary season, a way of almost uninterrupted suffering — which Ellicott calls in all ages the royal road to true greatness. As to how the account survived, he reports Ewald's suggestion that when in after years David drew the posterity of Jonathan to his court, he told them himself of these last events before the separation, there being no one but the two friends who could have known them.
9:
Jonathan's reply is a repudiation, and its grammar is construed two ways. Gill takes the disclaimer to be against the suspicion itself — that David should entertain such a thought of him, or have the least suspicion that he would conceal his father's ill intentions if he knew them. Keil and Delitzsch refer the exclamation back to what precedes, so that what is put far away is the killing or the handing over; and on the clause that follows they argue for reading an oath rather than a question. Because of the conjunction standing before the negative, they prefer to take it as an asseveration with the formula of swearing understood — if he discovers that evil is determined and does not tell it, then may God do so to him — rather than as the interrogative rendering, shall I not tell thee?

Ellicott reads the same words for their tone rather than their syntax. The strong expression bears emphatic testimony to Jonathan's implicit belief in his friend's stainless loyalty, and he indignantly refuses either to take that life himself or to allow it to be touched by his father. Ellicott notices the form the speech takes: the sentences here are broken ones, the next being left incomplete in the Hebrew, and he reads the breakage as a sign of the agitation and deep feeling of a chivalrous and indignant speaker.

Henry explains why a renewal of the friendship was needed at all. Notwithstanding David's strong confidence in Jonathan, he might have had some reason to fear that a father's influence and his own interest would make him warp or grow cool; so Jonathan thought it requisite to renew the professions of his friendship solemnly. Henry paraphrases the whole speech in that light — far be it from thee to think I suspect thee of any crime for which I should either slay thee myself or deliver thee to my father — and construes the invitation that follows accordingly: Jonathan did not challenge David to the field to fight him for an affront, but to fix him in his friendship.

What Jonathan undertakes is a report either way, and Henry presses the symmetry. He faithfully promised to let David know how he found his father affected on trial, and to make the matter neither better nor worse than it was: if there were good towards him he would tell him, that he might be easy; if evil, he would send him away, that he might be safe. Henry's summary is that between them these two undertakings would deliver David both from the evil, if it were real, and from the fear of evil, if it proved imaginary. Keil and Delitzsch record the practical objection David raises against the whole plan, asking who will tell him how Saul expresses himself, and what will happen if Jonathan's father answers roughly.
10:
David's objection is practical, and every witness grants it is a shrewd one. Gill and Clarke both read the question as asking by what means the intelligence could reach him — who will give the necessary information, and how will it be conveyed. Keil and Delitzsch supply the reasoning behind it and Ellicott quotes them for it: David's questions were suggested by a correct estimate of the circumstances, namely that Saul's suspicions would lead him to conclude there was some understanding between Jonathan and David, and that he would take steps accordingly to prevent Jonathan from passing on the result of the conversation. The plan as it stands depends on a messenger Saul could be expected to intercept.

The second half of the question is harder, and the Hebrew is broken. Ellicott describes the language as very abrupt and involved, and takes that as a mark of authenticity — evidently the very words uttered in the memorable scene by the excited and sorrowful friends are remembered and reported. He judges the conditional supplied in the English Version probably nearest the intended sense, while recording another rendering that reverses the clauses: if thy father shall answer thee harshly, who will declare it to me? Keil and Delitzsch read the clause as supposing Jonathan might attempt the errand himself, and they adjudicate between commentators — following De Wette and Maurer, and rejecting the construction of Gesenius and Thenius, who take the particle to mean if perchance. Their ground is that even where that rendering is possible it only arises when some other case is being supposed, so that the disjunctive sense still lies at the foundation.

The move out of doors is explained by what the palace could not offer. Gill has them going out so that they might talk of the affair more fully, freely and familiarly, without danger of being overheard by the servants of Saul in whose palace they then were. Keil and Delitzsch say Jonathan asked this before replying at all, so that they might there fix upon a sign by which he could convey the state of his father's mind without anyone suspecting; Ellicott describes the destination as a solitary spot where, before saying their last words together, they might agree upon some secret token. Clarke marks the same transition as the answer to David's question.

Henry turns the undertaking into a reflection on friendship. Jonathan faithfully promises to let David know how he finds his father affected, and Henry generalises: it will be kindness to ourselves and to ours to secure an interest in those whom God favours, and to make his friends ours. True friendship, he adds, rests on a firm basis and is able to silence ambition, self-love and undue regard for others — and from there he turns to the love of Christ, who gave himself as a sacrifice for rebellious and polluted sinners, asking how great the force and effects of our love to him and to his people ought therefore to be.
12:
Keil and Delitzsch set out the structure of what follows before examining any part of it. In the field, where the two were entirely free from observation, Jonathan first renewed his covenant with David by vowing on oath that he would report his father's feelings; then entreated him, with a certain presentiment that David would one day be king, to maintain his love towards him and his family for ever; then made David swear again concerning that love; and only last gave him the sign by which the promised information would be conveyed. They note that the two opening verses of the oath are connected, and that Jonathan begins with a solemn invocation of God.

That invocation is textually defective, and every witness says so. Gill treats the words as the form of an oath, and reports Jarchi and Kimchi for the sense by the Lord God of Israel, I swear unto thee. Clarke states plainly that something is evidently wanting, and lists what the versions supply — the Septuagint that the Lord God of Israel doth know, the Syriac and Arabic that he is witness — before preferring a reading found in two of Kennicott's manuscripts which inserts the word liveth, so that the whole becomes an oath formula with its apodosis following. He judges that to make the best sense of the three.

Ellicott surveys the same options and explains why the English will not do. The vocative rendering has been generally looked upon as an impossible one, there being no analogy for such a mode of address; the versions avoid it by supplying different words, and others supply the word found in the Hebrew manuscripts Clarke cites. Ellicott's own position is that the meaning is perfectly clear whichever supplement is adopted. Wesley alone defends the abruptness rather than repairing it, reading the words as an appeal to God to hear and judge between them, and observing that such an abrupt speech is usual in great passions.

The timetable in the oath confirms a point made earlier about the festival. Ellicott observes that Jonathan's statement of time evidently assumes the feast was continued the day after the new moon by a royal banquet, and he counts the days out: the present day, the morrow which was the new moon festival, and the day after that, which reckons as the third. On the substance of the undertaking Keil and Delitzsch keep to what the verse makes conditional — that if there be good towards David and Jonathan then fails to send and show it him, the unspoken penalty of the oath falls on Jonathan himself.
13:
The oath carries its own penalty clause, and Gill spells out what Jonathan is invoking: that the Lord recompense evil upon him, more than can be thought of or expressed, should he neglect to inform David of a good disposition in Saul. Keil and Delitzsch take the second branch as the more important undertaking — if it please Saul to do David evil, Jonathan will show him and send him away, that he may go in peace — so that the promise covers the bad outcome as fully as the good.

The blessing Jonathan adds is read as an admission. Clarke fastens on the wish that the Lord be with David as he had been with Saul, and concludes that from this and other passages here it is evident Jonathan knew the Lord had appointed David to the kingdom. The force of the remark is that Jonathan is the heir, and that the words concede the succession away from himself before anything has happened to make it inevitable.

What Jonathan asks in return is stated twice over, for himself and for his family. Gill glosses the kindness of the Lord as kindness well pleasing in God's sight, which imitates what he shows to men and which had been covenanted and agreed in his presence — and he notes that Jonathan did not doubt of this for himself, and therefore did not make it a request. Clarke puts the asking plainly as a future-tense bargain: when David comes to the kingdom, if Jonathan is alive, he shall show him kindness and continue it to his family after him. Wesley makes explicit the danger being guarded against, that David should not kill him or his, as princes of a new line commonly killed the nearest relations of the line from which the kingdom had been transferred.

The Hebrew of these verses is disordered, and the commentators treat the disorder as evidence. Ellicott calls it again very confused, abrupt and ungrammatical, and attributes this to the violent emotion of the speaker — holding that we have David's own report of what passed, the words of his dead friend having impressed themselves with a sad accuracy on his heart. On the text itself Ellicott reports a widely followed emendation, adopted from the Syriac and Arabic by Maurer, Ewald, Keil, Lange and others, which changes the negative in the first two clauses into an interjection of wishing. The resulting sense is a plea rather than a statement: that David would, while Jonathan still lives, show him the favour of the Lord, and if he dies would not withdraw that favour from his house for ever — not even when the LORD shall have cut off the enemies of David, every one, from the face of the earth.
15:
The pledge widens from the man to his descendants, and the witnesses mark the widening. Gill reads the clause as securing that Jonathan's household should partake of the kindness along with himself, and says as much of the compact that follows — it was struck not with David alone, whose own bond was merely being renewed, but with his kindred too. Wesley presents the transaction as reciprocal enlargement: what had been personal Jonathan now stretched over the whole line of David, expecting a matching extension on the other side, which Wesley has no doubt he obtained. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same act from the prince's end, that he concluded an agreement with David's posterity by drawing from him a promise of lasting favour, and they note that the governing noun must be supplied in thought to the verb.

The closing clause is construed two ways. Wesley hears an imprecation the parties call down upon themselves: should Jonathan or any of his line violate the terms and turn hostile, let the Lord, who witnessed the whole, punish the offender severely. Ellicott restructures the sentence instead, arguing it is unnecessary to insert the word of speech the English Version adds, and better to take the words as an aside dropped into the dialogue by the narrator — yielding the literal sense that Jonathan bound himself to David's posterity, and Jehovah required it at the hand of David's enemies. On that construction the line is no part of the vow at all but the historian's verdict on how it turned out.

The second adjuration reverses the parts. Gill explains its direction: having himself undertaken friendship towards David and his descendants, the prince pressed for a matching assurance in his own favour. Wesley terms this a restipulation, Jonathan having bound himself in the preceding verse and here exacting David's word in return. Keil and Delitzsch render the whole as an adjuring by affection — once more, and most earnestly, Jonathan implored his friend to deal graciously with him and with those who came after him, loving him as he loved his own soul.

Ellicott notices which man is petitioning the other, and why that is remarkable. All through this touching interview it is the prince who plays suppliant to the outlaw for his future good offices; Jonathan, foreseeing with absolute certainty the day when his persecuted friend would hold the throne and he himself lie in his grave, dreaded for his own fatherless children the end that too probably awaited them — it having been in every age a common usage in the East, when a dynasty was violently overturned, to put to death the offspring and near relations of the displaced king. Wesley supplies the motive the verse itself names: having a true affection for David, he wished the terms inviolably observed through all their generations.
18:
With the covenant concluded Jonathan returns to the practical matter. Gill notes only that tomorrow is the first day of the month, as David had already observed; Ellicott catches the change of register, paraphrasing the prince as resuming after the passionate conclusion of the compact — the trial shall be as David proposes, his seat at the royal banquet will be empty as agreed, and when Saul misses him the two of them will know the worst. Keil and Delitzsch give the clause its setting, that the empty place is at Saul's table.

Where David was to wait is described by reference to an earlier occasion. Gill supposes the three days were spent away from court, most probably at Bethlehem or elsewhere unrecognised, and argues it cannot have been in the field where he proposed to hide, since he could not have stayed there so long for want of food. Wesley identifies the former occasion precisely, as the time when this same business of discovering Saul's mind was in agitation before, and takes the landmark to be a stone that directs travellers on their way, David's station being some cave or convenient place near it.

Two words in the instruction give trouble, and both are treated at length. On the first, Keil and Delitzsch concede that the sense on the third day cannot be sustained from parallel passages, but hold it fully established partly by the related adjective and partly by Arabic usage. On the second they admit the difficulty is greater still, the verb with its adverb meaning literally to go violently down, yet they decline to question the correctness of the text. Ellicott pushes further and rejects the English outright: quickly comes from the Vulgate and does not render the Hebrew faithfully, the literal sense being greatly. He prefers Payne Smith's version — on the third day go a long way down into the valley — and reports that the word has been a general stumbling-block, the Chaldee, Arabic and Syriac interpreting rather than translating it as thou wilt be missed the more.

Ellicott also gives the reasoning that decides between the two senses, and it is a practical one. It did not matter whether David went fast or slow, since he was to hide there some time; what mattered was that he should be far away, so that no prying eye might chance to catch sight of him. On the phrase describing the earlier occasion Ellicott is candid that it is hard to understand, and settles for the rendering adopted by Gesenius, De Wette and Maurer, who translate it quite literally as on the day of the deed and take the deed to be Saul's own action against David.
20:
The signal agreed on is a piece of theatre with a servant for its unwitting instrument. Clarke sets out the whole device: David was to stay at the stone, where there was probably some cave or hiding place; Jonathan, to prevent all suspicion, would not approach him himself but would take his servant into the fields and pretend to be exercising himself in archery; the three arrows were shot the better to cover the design; and the words spoken to the boy who fetched them would carry the message. Gill accounts for the number, three being settled on according to the number of days David was missing. Wesley describes the mechanics from Jonathan's side — he would send the lad out before shooting, to find and take up the arrows, and would shoot either short of him or beyond him as he saw occasion.

Keil and Delitzsch render the two messages and their guarantees. If the word is that the arrows lie on this side of the boy, David is to come, for peace is to him and it is nothing, as truly as Jehovah liveth; if the arrows are said to lie beyond him, David is to go, for Jehovah sendeth him away — which they gloss as bidding him flee. Their verdict on the arrangement is that it was just as simple as it was suitable to its purpose.

A small textual oddity in the arrangement draws a note. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the arrows carry the definite article, and offer two explanations — either the historian assumed the thing already well known, or Jonathan went to the field armed and, in giving the sign, pointed to the arrows in his quiver. They add a remark on the pointing of the suffix in the word for side, where the diacritic indicates that the ending is not merely toneless despite lacking its usual mark, the strong breathing having been given up on account of the harsh consonant before it.

Ellicott notices that the plan as finally fixed is not quite the plan first proposed. Earlier it seemed as though Jonathan meant to send a special messenger if the news were good, whereas the arrangement now is that in either event he should come himself out from the city into the solitary valley. He also dissents from Payne Smith on a detail, who conceives the arrows were to be aimed at the stone itself: the description rather points to the mark as situated on the side of the stone, in or behind which David was to be concealed. On Ellicott's account the prince agreed to leave the city after the feast as though to practise at a mark, bringing with him a servant — probably one of his young armour-bearers.
22:
The second branch of the signal is the one that matters, and the witnesses keep it plain. Gill glosses the words about the arrows lying beyond the lad as meaning they had been shot to a greater distance than where he stood. Keil and Delitzsch render the message and its warrant together — if the word is that the arrows lie farther off, David is to go, for Jehovah sendeth him away, which they take to mean bids him flee. Their judgment on the device as a whole is that it was as simple as it was suitable to its purpose.

What the closing verse refers to is disputed only in extent. Gill takes the matter spoken of to be the covenant made between the two men and their families. Keil and Delitzsch argue for the wider reference, holding that the word points not merely to the sign agreed upon but to the whole business, including the renewal of the bond of friendship — and they add that the arrangement was to remain an eternal secret between them.

The invocation at the end is read as a legal formula. Keil and Delitzsch supply what the sentence leaves unsaid: the Lord stands between the two for ever as witness and judge, should either break the covenant, and they point for comparison to an earlier covenant sealed the same way (Genesis 31:48). They are careful to say this is implied by the words as they stand, so that there is no need to assume a word for witness has dropped out of the text. Wesley gives the same sense and extends it to the next generation — a witness and a judge between them and their families for ever, if on either side the league of friendship should be violated.

On David's going into hiding both Gill and Wesley enter a qualification about the timing. He did not conceal himself directly but at the time appointed, having first gone to Bethlehem and returned before the hour; Wesley says it seems probable he went there first and came back to the field when the occasion required. Keil and Delitzsch set the two men's movements side by side — David concealed himself in the field while Jonathan, as agreed, set about apologising for his absence from the king's table.
24:
The seating arrangement is described because one place in it is empty. Keil and Delitzsch note that Saul sat as always at his seat by the wall, which they explain as the top of the table — just as in eastern lands to this day the place of honour is the seat in the corner. Ellicott records only that the Septuagint paraphrases the verb, giving came to the table. Henry observes that every man knew his place but David's was vacant, and adds that it did not use to be so: none had been more content than he in attending holy duties, nor would he have been absent now but that he must have come at the peril of his life.

Henry draws a rule from the absence and then qualifies Saul's piety sharply. Self-preservation obliged David to withdraw, and in imminent peril present opportunities may be waived — indeed we ought not to throw ourselves into the mouth of danger, Christ himself having absconded often until he knew his hour was come. Against that Henry sets the king's own state of mind: Saul sat down to feast upon the peace-offerings as at other times, with his heart as full of envy and malice against David as it could hold. He should first have been reconciled and then have come and offered his gift, whereas instead he hoped at this very feast to drink David's blood — which makes the sacrifice an abomination, brought with such a mind as that (Proverbs 21:27).

A difficult clause about Jonathan and Abner occupies Keil and Delitzsch at length. They can hardly understand it otherwise than that when Abner entered, Jonathan rose from his seat beside Saul and gave the place up to him, in which case all that is missing from the record is a note of where Jonathan moved to. They defend that reading on comparative grounds, holding that every other attempted explanation is exposed to much graver difficulties, and they reject in particular Gesenius's proposal to supply a conjunction before Abner's name and refer the verb elsewhere. Henry reads the same moment simply as courtesy, Jonathan rising in reverence to Saul both as a father and as his sovereign.

What Saul said to himself on the first day is read as evidence of how well he knew David. Henry has him supposing some ceremonial pollution had befallen him, forbidding him to eat of the holy things until he had washed his clothes and bathed his flesh and been unclean until the evening; and the inference Henry draws is that Saul knew what conscience David made of the law, and that he would rather keep away from the holy feast than come in his uncleanness. Henry closes on the contrast for his own readers, that no uncleanness is now a restraint upon us but what may by faith and repentance be washed away in the fountain opened.
25:
The table is small enough that one absence shows. Clarke reconstructs it as a single table for Saul, Jonathan, David and Abner, with Saul holding the chief seat next to the wall, and remarks that with only four seated there the absence of any one would soon be noticed. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both explain why that seat was the chief one — in eastern lands the place of honour is the corner, or, as Ellicott puts it, the position opposite the door. Gill keeps to the plain sense, that Saul sat upon the seat he usually sat on.

The clause about Jonathan rising has no agreed construction, and Ellicott surveys the field. The Septuagint translates from a different text, making Saul go before Jonathan, which Keil dismisses as the senseless rendering of the Greek Version. Ellicott himself prefers the explanation of Abarbanel and Rashi: Jonathan, having already seated himself after his father, saw that David's place was noticed, rose, and seated Abner at Saul's side in the vacant place, so that the seat next the king should not stand empty — taking for himself the seat on the other side. He notes that this reading requires the verb to be causative, written defectively, and cites a parallel for the form.

Keil and Delitzsch reach almost the same picture with a different emphasis. They can hardly read the passage otherwise than that when Abner entered, Jonathan rose from his seat beside Saul and gave up the place to him, with only a note of where Jonathan then moved missing from the record; and they defend this on the ground that every other attempted explanation runs into much graver difficulties, rejecting in particular Gesenius's proposal to supply a conjunction before Abner's name.

Saul's silence on the first day is explained by a ceremonial rule. Keil and Delitzsch have him supposing something had befallen David to make him unclean, and point to the laws on the subject; Wesley specifies the consequence, that such an accident would render him unfit to partake of a feast consisting in part of the remainders of the peace offerings, and unfit also to come into any company, much more the king's, lest he pollute them too. Gill notes only that Saul said nothing at all about the absence and took no notice of it — which, given what the next day brings, is itself the point.
27:
Why there was a second day of feasting at all is explained two ways. Gill reports the Targum's reading, that the day after was the intercalation of the second month, and gives the mechanism: when the beginning of the month was judged by the appearance of the moon and there was difficulty about which day it had appeared on, two days were kept — Abarbinel being clear that two were kept in this month. But Gill offers an alternative that does not need the intercalation, since the remainder of the peace offerings might be eaten the following day, so Saul and his guests might have met on the second day for that purpose. Keil and Delitzsch settle a grammatical point in the same verse, that the ordinal is a nominative belonging to the opening verb rather than a genitive attached to the word for new moon.

The second absence is what breaks the silence, and Ellicott explains the logic of it. David's continued absence awoke Saul's suspicion, and he questioned the son sitting beside him, being aware that no accident of ceremonial defilement would keep a man away two days running. Wesley makes the same point from the rule, that uncleanness contracted by some chance usually lasted only for one day. Both Wesley and Henry notice how the king refers to the missing man: he calls him the son of Jesse in scorn, to mark the meanness of his origin and as not deigning to use his proper name — Henry adding the irony that David was Saul's own son by marriage.

Henry reads the question itself as capable of an innocent construction, and uses it before turning it. Saul asks as though displeased that anyone should be absent from a religious feast, which Henry makes an example to masters of families, to see that those under their charge are not absent from the worship of God, whether in public or in the family; and he warns that except in case of necessity it is a bad thing to omit an opportunity of attending on God in solemn ordinances, Thomas having lost a sight of Christ by being once absent from a meeting of the disciples. What actually displeased Saul, Henry concludes, was that he had missed the opportunity he expected of doing David a mischief.

The answer Jonathan gives is the one agreed on in advance. Keil and Delitzsch note the correspondence with the earlier arrangement clause by clause, and gloss the reference to the brother as the elder brother, then at the head of the family and the man who arranged the sacrificial meal. Henry sets out the excuse as a two-part defence — that David was absent on a good occasion, keeping the feast elsewhere at the summons of an elder brother now more respectful to him than he had once been, and that he had not gone without leave humbly asked and obtained from Jonathan, his superior officer, which represents David as wanting in no instance of respect or duty to the government.
30:
The excuse produces exactly the result David had predicted. Gill reports the anger as kindled for giving David leave to go and for excusing him in that manner. Ellicott reconstructs what the explosion reveals: probably Saul had determined at that very feast, surrounded by his own devoted friends and family, to carry out his designs against David's life, so that murder was one of the incidents arranged for at the banquet, and the absence of the intended victim marred the plot. He adds a second cause of rage, that with the cunning the partially insane so often display, Saul saw through the specious excuse — perceiving that David too clearly suspected the design and had purposely stayed away, and that his own son and heir suspected him too, and openly sympathised with the friend whose pointed absence he had just publicly apologised for.

The insult Saul throws is read as aimed past Jonathan at his mother. Keil and Delitzsch render it son of a perverse and rebellious woman, and note that the slight is offered to the mother and is therefore so much the greater to the son. Clarke collects the renderings and finds them various — the Hebrew might be turned son of an unjust rebellion, that is, thou art a rebel against thy own father, while the Vulgate and the Septuagint both produce versions implying something discreditable in the woman's own conduct. Clarke observes that if those were the sense, the reflection must refer to some secret transaction between Saul and Jonathan's mother, which reflects more dishonour on himself than on his brave son — and he draws the general rule that most sarcasms bear as hard upon the speaker as on the man they are aimed at, abusive language always arguing a mean, weak and malevolent heart.

Ellicott prefers a reading that removes the mother from the sentence altogether. The word rendered perverse is probably not a feminine adjective but an abstract noun, so that the phrase becomes son of perversity of rebellion — a common Hebraism for a man of perverse and refractory nature. On either construction, he notes, the words spoken in public were a bitter insult to the prince.

The charge underneath the abuse is dynastic. Wesley reads the taunt about confusion as a prediction of what people will say — that Jonathan has no royal blood in his veins, who can so tamely give up his crown to so contemptible a person.
31:
Ellicott hears in the threat the fixed idea of a diseased mind. The thought ever torturing Saul was that David — his own kind physician, his faithful soldier, and his son's dearest friend and companion — was plotting basely against the master for whom he had done so much and the son he loved so well. In his blind fury the king then betrays the purpose outright with the words that David shall surely die; and Ellicott reads the accompanying command to send and fetch him as proof that the murder had been pre-arranged for the feast, since those rough soldier chiefs sitting round the royal table would be ready at any moment to carry out their master's savage behest.

Gill sets out the reasoning Saul presses on his son. As heir to the crown Jonathan would not be sure of it while David lived: his tenure would be precarious, and in great danger of being taken from him at his father's death — so that on Saul's argument it would be Jonathan's highest wisdom to deliver David up to be slain, and his greatest folly to protect him and provide for his safety.

Jonathan's reply is a question, not a defence. Keil and Delitzsch render it simply — my father, why shall he die, what has he done? — and treat it as the trigger for what follows. The question asks for a charge, and the answer it receives is the javelin.

The throw settles the matter Jonathan had been unwilling to believe. Keil and Delitzsch note that Saul was so enraged he hurled his javelin at his own son, and compare the earlier occasion on which he had done the same to David; from which Jonathan saw that his father had firmly resolved to put David to death. They gloss the word for that resolve as a noun meaning an unalterable determination, the same root used earlier in the chapter when the test was first proposed.

What Jonathan does next is reported as a double reaction. He rose from the table in fierce anger and ate nothing that day — and Keil and Delitzsch are careful about the cause, that the grief was for David, because his father had done him shame. The shame in question is therefore not the insult Jonathan himself had just received but the treatment of his friend, which is what the narrative chooses to record. Keil and Delitzsch add the dating, that this was the second day of the new moon.
32:
What Jonathan answers, and what he lets pass, is itself noticed. Gill observes that he made no answer at all to the charges of perverseness, rebellion and folly brought against himself, which he bore with patience, but could not bear to hear his friend spoken against and declared worthy of death. Ellicott reads the attempt as a repetition of something that had worked before: remembering the effect of his quiet, earnest remonstrance on a previous occasion, Jonathan again tried to deprecate his father's unreasoning jealous anger — but this time to no purpose, a paroxysm of madness seizing Saul, who grasped the long spear leaning at his side and raised the great war weapon to strike down his son.

The spear at Saul's side prompts a note on royal custom. Gill infers from the incident that Saul always had a javelin in his hand, and accounts for it from the manner of the times: in other countries as well as this, kings carried spears instead of sceptres and used them as such. He cites Justin, who says that in the days of Romulus kings had spears as an ensign of royalty, which the Greeks call sceptres — adding that the Greeks in turn called sceptres spears. Wesley draws a different lesson from the same throw, that Saul had seemed to be in great care for Jonathan's establishment in the kingdom and now aims at his life, which prompts his exclamation on what fools, and what worse than savage beasts, anger makes of men.

What the throw proved is stated without qualification. Keil and Delitzsch have Jonathan knowing from it that his father had firmly resolved to put David to death — the test David had asked for was complete, and its answer was unambiguous.

The anger Jonathan then shows is read for its object, and there the readings part company. Ellicott takes the record at its word and allows two causes, first the terrible insult offered to the prince and heir before the assembled great ones of Israel, with the uplifted spear following the harsh words in an act not likely to be soon forgotten by the spectators; and second the determined and relentless enmity against David, of whose stainless integrity Jonathan was firmly convinced — of which Ellicott thinks the wrong to his friend affected him most. Gill names both too, the attempt to smite him and the resolution to slay David. Clarke dissents from the translation itself, suggesting we should understand the phrase rather of Jonathan's grief than of his anger, the following clause explaining the former: he was grieved for his father, and he was grieved for his friend.
35:
The signal is carried out exactly as rehearsed. Gill dates it to the morning of the third day of the month; Ellicott remarks that the meeting is not described at any length, since all was done as pre-arranged and everything had come to pass as David in his sad foresight had expected. Keil and Delitzsch say the same of the narrative's economy, that the account of the sign and of the meeting which followed is given very concisely, only the main points being touched upon; and they canvass the renderings of the phrase describing Jonathan's going out, which may mean at the time agreed with David, or to the meeting with David.

Henry narrates the device in motion. Jonathan went at the time and to the place appointed, within sight of which he knew David lay hid, sent his footboy to fetch the arrows he would shoot at random, and gave the fatal signal by shooting an arrow beyond the lad. Henry's observation on the words called out is the sharpest thing in the passage: that term beyond, David knew the meaning of better than the lad did. Gill adds that Jonathan had no doubt told the boy which mark he would shoot at, and bid him look about there for them.

Only one arrow is mentioned where three had been agreed, and the discrepancy is addressed. Keil and Delitzsch explain the singular as used with indefinite generality, the historian not considering it necessary to state expressly, after what he had already written, that Jonathan shot three arrows one after another; and they note a grammatical peculiarity, that the form of the word used here occurs only in connection with disjunctive accents. Ellicott follows them, and rejects the alternative explanation outright: we cannot imagine that Jonathan shortened the affair and shot only once because there was danger in delay, since had there been such need of haste the parting scene itself would have been cut shorter.

The mechanics of the shot are given plainly by Keil and Delitzsch — the boy ran, and Jonathan shot so that the arrows flew farther than the boy had run. Henry completes the sequence: Jonathan dismissed the lad, who knew nothing of the matter, and then, finding the coast clear and no danger of discovery, presumed upon one minute's personal conversation with David after he had already bidden him flee for his life. Henry marks what that minute was worth, this being the sorrowful parting of two friends who, so far as appears, never came together again but once, and that by stealth in a wood.
37:
The words called after the lad carry two meanings at once, and the commentators separate them. Keil and Delitzsch render the first as the agreed signal — see, the arrow lies away from thee, farther off — and the second as an urgency about the boy himself, quickly, haste, do not stand still, given so that he might not see David, who was somewhere near. Clarke insists the urgency was not really addressed to the servant at all: though the words appear to be spoken to the lad, they were spoken to David, indicating that his life was at stake and that only a prompt flight could save him. Gill reads them a third way, as meant simply to get the arrows back quickly so that Jonathan might dismiss the boy, having observed that nobody was passing and wanting a few minutes alone with his friend before the flight.

The lad's ignorance is recorded deliberately. Gill spells out what he did not know — what was meant by the shooting of the arrows, by their being shot beyond where he stood, and by the order to make haste in bringing them. Keil and Delitzsch note that the writer introduces this remark at just this point, and Ellicott observes that although Jonathan trusted the youth to a certain extent, probably an armour-bearer, he still hurried him away so that he should not see David and the meeting should go unwitnessed. On the text Keil and Delitzsch judge the written form the original reading, with the singular to be understood as earlier in the chapter, the marginal reading being an emendation made to suit the sense.

Sending the weapons back with the boy served the same purpose. Keil and Delitzsch read it as a device to gain a few seconds, Jonathan giving the lad his bow, arrows and quiver and sending him to the town so that he might speak with David after his departure and take leave of him unobserved. Ellicott says the same, that the youth was sent to the city so Jonathan might be alone once more with his friend.

The word used for the weapons draws a note from three witnesses, all making the same point. Gill glosses it as his vessels or instruments, his arms, following the Targum in listing quiver, bow and arrows; Wesley gives the same three. Clarke makes the lexical observation that this is, he believes, the only place in the language where the English word used here is not applied to cannon or ordnance, the original signifying simply instruments. Ellicott agrees the literal sense is his implements, and judges that expressive though the old rendering is, it would scarcely now be used in this sense, the Hebrew being better translated by arms.
39:
The moment of meeting is described, and the direction David comes from is textually contested. Gill notes only that David could observe from his lurking place when the lad was gone. Keil and Delitzsch render the phrase as from the side of the south, and explain it as describing the hiding-place by its direction relative to where Jonathan was standing; they then observe that none of the early translators rendered it correctly except Aquila and Jerome, the Septuagint, Chaldee, Syriac and Arabic all simply repeating the earlier statement about the stone because their translators could not see the force of the words.

Ellicott is more doubtful still about the text and more interested in the staging. If the words are correct, which he thinks very doubtful, they must mean that as soon as David perceived Jonathan was alone he rose from the south side of the rock where he had lain concealed. He lists the variants — the Chaldee reading from the stone of the sign, one Septuagint manuscript giving a place name and another the word for sleep — and agrees that the versions have more or less repeated the earlier statement, failing altogether to understand the two Hebrew words. He adds the practical point that the arrow sign alone would have been enough to warn David, and that had he not seen Jonathan waiting for him he would have made his escape from hiding unseen.

What the two then do is reported in a sequence of acts. Keil and Delitzsch have David fall on his face to the ground and bow three times before Jonathan, after which they kissed each other and wept, until, as they render the last clause, David wept very loud. The obeisance is the detail that marks the relation: the man who has just been promised a throne prostrates himself three times before the prince who has given it up.

Clarke explains why the weeping should have been heaviest on David's side, and the reasons are cumulative. His distress must in the nature of things have been the greatest, for besides the friend he was now to lose for ever he was losing his wife, his relatives and his country — and, what Clarke calls most afflictive of all, the altars of his God and the ordinances of religion. Clarke then turns to the king: Saul saw David's growing popularity and was convinced of his own maladministration, but because he did not humble himself before God he became a prey to envy, pride, jealousy and cruelty. From such a man David had everything to fear, and thought it safer to yield to the storm than to brave it — though Clarke judges he could have raised a very powerful party in Israel had he used the means so much in his power. That he did not is Clarke's point: neither seeking nor affecting the kingdom, he left it to the providence of God to bring him in by such means and at such a time as was most suited.
42:
The parting word is a single sentence, and it is grammatically incomplete. Keil and Delitzsch note that all we are given of the conversation is Jonathan's farewell, and that the clause breaks off unfinished — what the two had sworn in the name of the LORD, that the LORD be between them and between their seed for ever. They identify the figure as an aposiopesis and account for it from Jonathan's deep emotion, the missing conclusion being recoverable from the sense: let it stand, or let us abide by it. They add a textual observation, that by comparison with the earlier verse the words for ever must be understood as forming part of the oath itself rather than of the comment on it.

Ellicott treats the abruptness as the most natural thing in the scene. It accords with the evident deep emotion of the speaker; and on David's side, his heart being too full to reply, he seems to have hurried away speechless, blinded with tears. On that reading the incompleteness of the sentence is not a defect to be repaired but the record of a man unable to finish what he was saying.

Gill reads the blessing as having a particular content rather than being a formula. To go in peace is to go in peace of mind, committing himself, his family and his affairs to the providence of God, who would keep him safe from Saul's designs; and Gill adds a second element, that Jonathan would have David easy about what had passed between the two of them, not doubting it would be faithfully observed on both sides. The farewell therefore discharges the anxiety the whole chapter has been about.

Ellicott closes with a judgment on the friendship, quoting Phillipson. We may indeed wonder at the delicacy of feeling and the gentleness of sentiment which these two men entertained for one another in those old rough times; no ancient writer has set before us so noble an example of a heartfelt, unselfish and thoroughly human state of feeling, nor described friendship with such entire truth in all its relations and such profound knowledge of the human heart. Keil and Delitzsch end on the bare movement instead — David set out upon his journey and Jonathan returned to the town — and remark that this verse ought strictly to form the conclusion of the chapter.
